items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: If it hadn’t been for King Pleasure, for Eddie Jefferson, for Annie Ross’ “Twisted” and “Farmer’s Market” which were done before Lambert, Hendricks & Ross, I would not have had the road sign to point me toward lyricizing orchestral versions of things.

ctx.x: That was my son. Well when you look in jazz history there’s a small number comparatively of real innovators. There’s people that build on the innovations. I think that you’re one of those small number of innovators and gosh, you can take a great deal of pride in that.

Well it’s delicate for me because you must be aware of egoism. Egoism — or is it egotism — I don’t know if there’s a “t” in there or not, and I’m an English major I should know. But anyway you must beware of the ego, the overactivity of the ego. Because man nothing is done alone. items.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He says, “I’d like you to record something with me.”

ctx.x: Had you met – when did you meet King Pleasure?

I met him when he – I was in the Turf bar at 52nd and Broadway. We all used to hang out in there, all the songwriters and performers. He came in. Somebody introduced me to him. I said, “Oh man.” I said, “You started me writing like that.” He says, “Yeah. That’s what I want to talk to you about.” I says, “What is that?” He says, “I’d like you to record something with me.” He says, “I have this Stan Getz tune that he recorded in Sweden called Don’t Get Scared.
“When you see danger facing you, little boy don’t get scared.”

items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: He has taken the vocalese style of singing pioneered by King Pleasure and Eddie Jefferson to a virtuoso level

ctx.x: Vocalist Jon Hendricks was born in Newark, Ohio in 1921. He has taken the vocalese style of singing pioneered by King Pleasure and Eddie Jefferson to a virtuoso level and is a household name with jazz fans around the world. His unique re-working of Basie standards with Lambert, Hendricks and Ross and later Joe Williams, established a new style of vocal jazz in the late 50s and this trio recorded such classic tunes as “Cloudburst,” “Gimme That Wine” and “Centerpiece.” His production “Evolution of the Blues” became…
Jon was interviewed in New York City by Monk Rowe on October 18, 1995.
